newsitem.title: USA: MGI Pharma says drug studies positive.
newsitem.headline: MGI Pharma says drug studies positive.

text.p: MGI Pharma Inc, a specialty pharmaceutical company, said Tuesday a phase III trial of its drug showed positive results in treating symptoms of dry mouth and dry eyes in patients suffering from Sjogren's syndrome.
MGI said that based on these results, it will seek marketing approval for its Salagen tablets from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration before the end of 1996 or very early in 1997.
MGI said it has no assurance that FDA approval will be granted.
Results of MGI's studies were presented at an International Dry Eye Conference held this week in Bermuda. MGI conducted

two double-blind, placebo-controlled studies that involved 629 Sjogren's syndrome patients. In the studies, patients taking its Salagen tablets showed improvements in sleeping, eating, and talking, and experienced less discomfort in the eye, including less itching, redness and tiredness. The most common side effect from the drug was sweating; there were no serious adverse experiences reported.

Sjogren's syndrome is a chronic, inflammatory, autoimmune disease where the body's own immune system attacks the moisture producing glands, particularly the salivary and tear glands, causing them to lose their ability to produce saliva and tears. The resulting dryness can cause severe discomfort in the mouth and eyes. Primary Sjogren's syndrome affects about 200,000 people in the United States, most of whom are women over the age of 50.

Currently, Salagen tablets are marketed for the treatment of symptoms of dry mouth caused by radiation used in the treatment of head and neck cancers. It works by stimulating the moisture producing glands throughout the body, including the salivary and tear glands.
